method: The page reproduces the Brewers Association draught-beer carbonation chart: ten temperatures from 33 to 42 degrees Fahrenheit by eleven volumes from 2.1 to 3.1, each cell the equilibrium gauge pressure in psig for beer at specific gravity 1.015 and 4.8 percent ABV, from the ASBC Methods of Analysis, 5th edition (1949). Henry's law makes every row a straight line, so the eleven printed points of a row are fitted by least squares and a target volume is read from that line; 2.0 to 3.6 volumes are accepted, and a value outside 2.1-3.1 is reported as an extension of the row. A temperature between the printed rows is interpolated linearly between the two neighbouring fitted lines, and values outside 33-42 degrees Fahrenheit (0.6-5.6 degrees Celsius) are refused. Altitude follows the chart's own rule, adding 1 psi per 2,000 ft (609.6 m) above sea level, so the published 11.3 psig for 2.5 volumes at 38 degrees Fahrenheit becomes 13.3 psig at 4,000 ft. Outputs are the gauge pressure in psi to one decimal, the sea level share and the altitude addition, the same pressure in bar (0.0689475729 bar per psi) and kilopascals (6.894757293168 kPa per psi), and the dissolved gas in grams per litre at 1.9635 g per volume from the 44.0095 g/mol molar mass and the 22.41397 L/mol molar volume at 0 degrees Celsius. Blank, non-numeric and out-of-range entries are refused with a field-specific message. The page makes no network request and stores nothing, and it does not model bottle priming sugar, beer-line balancing or blended gas, which are separate jobs.

sources.title: Brewers Association, Facts About Draught Beer Carbonation - the equilibrium gauge pressure chart for 2.1-3.1 volumes of CO2 at 33-42 F (ASBC Methods of Analysis, 5th ed., 1949), with the worked 11.3 psig example and the +1 psig per 2,000 ft altitude rule

Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual (2022), Table 1 - the same pure CO2 equilibrium pressure table with its sea-level note, the 36-38 F serving band and the instruction to add 1 psi for every 2,000 ft of elevation
